items.title: Large-scale AI-guided liver malignancy diagnosis: multicenter study and a single-arm trial.
items.body: Liver malignancies are frequently evaluated on contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CE-CT), but missed or delayed diagnoses remain a clinically important challenge in high-volume, real-world radiology workflows, highlighting the need for scalable diagnostic safety net approaches. To address this, we developed the Liver DiagnOsis Network (LiON), a CE-CT-based artificial intelligence (AI) system that supports flexible multiphase processing, clinical data integration and workflow-compatible liver malignancy diagnosis. LiON was trained on 6,443 patients and retrospectively validated across 22,251 patients from multicenter and real-world cohorts. LiON achieved high performance for malignancy diagnosis, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.975 (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.971-0.979), and maintained robust performance in real-world cohorts and among patients with hepatic steatosis (AUC 0.971, 95% CI: 0.952-0.985) and cirrhosis (AUC 0.924, 95% CI: 0.901-0.946). We then conducted a single-arm trial in 10,333 patients in routine clinical practice, in which LiON functioned as an additional AI reader within the existing clinical workflow. The trial met its primary endpoint, defined as an AUC for malignancy diagnosis with the lower bound of the 95% CI exceeding 0.900, achieving an AUC of 0.952 (95% CI: 0.942-0.961). Secondary outcomes demonstrated that AI-human collaboration identified 51 previously overlooked lesions (15 malignancies) and triggered 37 amended radiology reports, 22 multidisciplinary team escalations and clinical management changes in a subset of patients. These findings suggest that AI, when deployed as a workflow-compatible diagnostic support, may help reduce missed or delayed diagnoses and guide clinical interventions. Nevertheless, further evidence from prospective comparative studies across diverse healthcare systems is warranted to assess effects on clinical outcomes. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT07153783 .
items.why: This large multicenter study developed LiON, a contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CE-CT) based AI system for liver malignancy diagnosis, validating it retrospectively across 22,251 patients (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) 0.975) and then testing it prospectively as an added reader in a single-arm trial of 10,333 patients, where it identified 51 previously overlooked lesions and prompted 22 multidisciplinary escalations. This is a rare example of AI moving from retrospective validation to real clinical workflow deployment with measurable downstream management changes, though it still needs a comparative prospective trial to establish outcome benefit.
items.plain: Researchers built an AI tool called LiON that reads CT scans to help diagnose liver cancer, tested it on over 22,000 patients in multiple hospitals with very high accuracy, and then used it in real clinical practice on more than 10,000 patients, where it caught 51 lesions doctors had missed and led to 22 cases being escalated for expert review. This shows AI actually changing what happens in patient care, not just performing well on paper, though a study comparing it directly against standard care is still needed to prove it improves outcomes.

glossary.definition: A CT scan enhanced with an injected dye that highlights blood vessels and tissue differences to improve diagnosis.

glossary.term: Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC)
glossary.definition: A number between 0.5 and 1 that measures how well a model distinguishes between people who will and will not have an outcome, where 1 is perfect and 0.5 is no better than chance.
A study where every participant receives the same intervention, with no separate comparison group.

items.title: A bimodal large language model reduces misalignment in patient education: A double-blinded randomized trial.
items.body: BACKGROUND: Effective patient education requires accurate communication aligned with patients' emotional and semantical needs. Text-based large language models (LLMs) lack access to non-verbal cues, which may contribute to misaligned responses. METHODS: We evaluated emotional and semantic misalignment in a text-based LLM using 64,200 utterances from 16,583 patient education cases across six departments and three centers. Dolphin was developed integrating text and audio cues and evaluated through emotion recognition, semantic consistency assessment, branch-level ablations, and a double-blinded randomized trial against a matched text-based LLM comparator (Chinese Clinical Trial Registry: (ChiCTR2500095933). FINDINGS: The text-based LLM showed emotional misalignment in 36.7% of responses and semantic misalignment in 28.3% of cases, with higher misalignment under greater burden. Dolphin outperformed the text-based LLM in emotion recognition accuracy (0.886 vs. 0.713) and semantic consistency (84.9% vs. 82.1%; both adjusted p < 0.001). Ablations supported contribution of audio branches. Dolphin received higher expert ratings than the text-based LLM and human educators (all p < 0.001). In 555 patients, Dolphin was associated with greater patient satisfaction (98.6% vs. 93.8%), suggestion acceptance (76.1% vs. 58.9%; p < 0.001), proactive disclosure (44.6% vs. 26.5%; p < 0.001), and fewer 7-day unplanned recontact (12.9% vs. 22.9%; p = 0.002). No unsafe recommendations or safety events were identified. CONCLUSIONS: Compared with text-based LLM, Dolphin improved emotional-semantic alignment and patient-education outcomes, supporting bimodal alignment as a strategy for reducing misalignment-driven communication failures. FUNDING: National Natural Science Foundation of China, State Key Laboratory Special Fund, and Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences Innovation Fund.
items.why: A double-blinded randomized controlled trial (RCT) tested a bimodal (text and audio) large language model (LLM), Dolphin, against a matched text-only LLM in patient education across 555 patients, finding higher patient satisfaction (98.6% vs 93.8%), greater suggestion acceptance (76.1% vs 58.9%), and fewer 7-day unplanned recontacts (12.9% vs 22.9%, p=0.002). This is a rare randomized trial with real clinical workload and satisfaction endpoints comparing an AI system against both a text-only AI and human educators, making it directly relevant evidence for whether multimodal cues improve patient communication.
items.plain: Scientists built an AI that listens to both the words and tone of voice of patients, then tested it in a randomized trial against a text-only AI chatbot with 555 real patients. The voice-aware AI led to higher patient satisfaction, more patients following its advice, and fewer people needing to come back within a week, which is a real measured benefit rather than just a quality score.

glossary.definition: A study design where participants are randomly assigned to different treatments and neither participants nor assessors know who got which, reducing bias.
An AI system that processes more than one type of input, such as both text and audio, rather than just text.

items.title: Prospective evaluation of a large language model clinical decision support system in the emergency department.
items.body: Prospective evidence for artificial intelligence (AI)-based clinical decision support in emergency departments remains limited. Here we conducted a DECIDE-AI stage 1 evaluation of SHAKED, a clinical decision support system built on multiple large language models, in a tertiary emergency department. Over 4 weeks, 1,138 patients were analyzed across two parallel units-one using SHAKED and one following routine rotations. Clinical adoption of SHAKED declined from 68% to 30%, owing to workload-sensitive disengagement (OR = 0.72 per shift hour, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.83). Physicians preferred the use of SHAKED for radiology consultations (OR = 2.98, 95% CI 1.58 to 5.63). No adverse events were detected, and expert review rated 99 of 100 sampled outputs as clinically appropriate. Emergency department length of stay did not differ between wings (4.9 h in both, P = 0.99). Intention-to-treat analysis showed a non-significant trend toward shorter consultation cycle time (-9.4 min, P = 0.077). These findings suggest that sustained clinician engagement, rather than algorithmic accuracy, may be the key barrier to effective clinical AI use in emergency departments. They inform randomized trial design but do not justify clinical deployment of AI clinical decision support at this stage. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06902675 .
items.why: In this DECIDE-AI stage 1 prospective evaluation, an emergency department deployed SHAKED, a large language model (LLM) based clinical decision support system, across 1,138 patients over four weeks, finding declining physician adoption (68% to 30%) tied to workload rather than any measured harm, with no significant change in length of stay. The key finding, that sustained clinician engagement rather than algorithmic accuracy is the bottleneck for AI adoption in acute care, is directly relevant to this reader's interest in how LLMs perform in real clinical use rather than in benchmark settings.
items.plain: Doctors in an emergency department tried out an AI assistant called SHAKED for four weeks, and while the AI's answers were judged safe and accurate almost every time, doctors used it less and less as their shifts got busier, dropping from 68% usage to 30%. The study found that patients did not spend less time in the hospital because of the AI, suggesting that getting doctors to actually keep using AI tools day to day, not whether the AI itself works well, is the real challenge.

glossary.definition: An early-stage framework for testing AI decision support tools in real clinical settings before larger trials, focused on safety and usability.
A type of AI trained on large amounts of text that can generate humanlike written responses.
A number comparing how much more or less likely an event is in one group versus another, where 1 means no difference.

items.title: Patient-Facing AI System for Symptom Guidance Using Simulated Encounters and Physician Review: Analytical Validation Study.
items.body: BACKGROUND: Rapid advances in large language models (LLMs) have expanded interest in patient-facing health applications that support symptom assessment and care-seeking decisions. Although AI-enabled symptom-guidance tools could improve patient navigation and recognition of clinically serious conditions, inappropriate recommendations may result in missed needed care or unnecessary escalation. Structured predeployment evaluation is therefore needed before prospective clinical use. OBJECTIVE: This formative predeployment study aimed to analytically validate a locked configuration of the Personal Health Assistant (PHA; Verily Health), an LLM-enabled patient-facing symptom-guidance tool, under controlled conditions using simulated patient encounters and expert physician review. METHODS: We conducted a prospective predeployment analytical validation study using synthetic patient data. The analysis set included 772 synthetic cases generated using published telephone-triage protocols and persona-based, LLM-assisted case generation. Each case included a clinical vignette, structured medical history information, and a simulated multiturn patient conversation. All cases were reviewed by a panel of 5 independent physicians without access to PHA outputs in order to provide level-of-care recommendations. Case-level ground truth was derived from aggregated physician ratings using prespecified plurality and tie-handling rules. Urgent undertriage, nonurgent undertriage, and overtriage were evaluated against prespecified performance criteria. Secondary analyses assessed the clinical appropriateness of PHA-generated possible conditions and escalation, self-care, and laboratory-testing recommendations. RESULTS: The final analysis set contained 772 cases, including 2 with unevaluable ground truth that were excluded from primary Endpoint denominators. Urgent undertriage was identified in 28 of 406 cases (6.9%, 95% CI 4.6%-9.8%), nonurgent undertriage in 56 of 305 (18.4%, 95% CI 14.2%-23.2%), and overtriage in 40 of 364 (11.0%, 95% CI 8.0%-14.7%). Overtriage met the prespecified criterion of less than 30%, whereas urgent and nonurgent undertriage did not meet their respective criteria of less than 5% and less than 15%, respectively. Secondary findings were generally supportive of the clinical appropriateness of the additional PHA outputs. CONCLUSIONS: PHA met the prespecified overtriage criterion but did not meet the urgent or nonurgent undertriage criteria. The findings identified undertriage as the principal performance gap requiring further product refinement. Because the study used synthetic cases, simulated conversations, and enriched urgency categories under controlled conditions, the results may not reflect performance in real-world populations or deployment settings. Prospective evaluation with actual users in the intended-use population is needed before broader clinical use.
items.why: A prospective predeployment validation study tested a locked configuration of a large language model (LLM)-enabled patient-facing symptom triage tool against 772 simulated cases with physician panel-derived ground truth, finding overtriage met the prespecified safety threshold (<30%) but urgent undertriage (6.9%) and nonurgent undertriage (18.4%) failed their respective thresholds. This is a real predeployment safety evaluation with quantified failure rates against explicit clinical criteria, directly relevant to assessing whether patient-facing symptom-guidance AI is safe enough for real use.
items.plain: Before releasing an AI symptom-checker tool to patients, researchers tested it on 772 simulated medical cases and compared its recommendations to what a panel of doctors said should happen. The tool was safe enough on over-caution but missed the safety bar for correctly flagging some urgent and less-urgent cases that needed care, showing a real limitation before deployment.

glossary.definition: A type of AI trained on large amounts of text that can generate humanlike written responses.
When a screening tool wrongly judges a case as less urgent than it actually is, risking delayed care.
When a screening tool wrongly judges a case as more urgent than it actually is, causing unnecessary escalation.
The accepted correct answer used to check whether a test or model got things right.

items.title: User evaluation of AI- and human-generated responses in digital health communication: a paired survey study.
items.body: BACKGROUND: Digital health communication is gaining importance as health care systems face increasing demand and structural constraints. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly used for health information seeking; however, direct comparisons between AI-generated and human responses from the user perspective remain limited. METHODS: A quantitative exploratory cross-sectional online survey using a paired-response design was conducted in Germany. The survey instrument was developed based on the study objectives and refined through pretesting. Participants evaluated two responses to the same real-world health query: one written by a physiotherapist and one generated by ChatGPT-4. Outcomes included perceived empathy, comprehensibility, perceived discriminatory content in the responses, and expert-rated clinical quality. Paired comparisons were analyzed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and logistic regression models were applied to explore associations between participant characteristics and preference patterns. RESULTS: The analytical sample comprised 224 participants. Across most items, the AI-generated response was rated more favorably than the human response, particularly with regard to comprehensibility and empathy (all p < .001). The AI-generated response was rated more favorably across both empathy and comprehensibility items, with highly comparable preference distributions between the two domains. Perceptions of discriminatory content were rare and did not differ significantly between responses. Expert evaluations also favored the AI-generated response in terms of clinical accuracy and completeness, although these findings should be interpreted cautiously given the exploratory design. CONCLUSIONS: The findings suggest that participants perceived the AI-generated response as aligning more closely with central user expectations for text-based health information, particularly regarding clarity and supportive language, although these findings should be interpreted cautiously given the substantial differences in length and structure between responses and the exploratory single-case design. At the same time, these perceptions should be considered alongside ongoing concerns regarding the clinical appropriateness, safety, and equity of AI-generated health information, which were not comprehensively assessed in the present study. The present findings therefore primarily provide evidence regarding user-perceived communication quality rather than the clinical validity of AI-generated responses. Accordingly, further research is needed to establish the clinical appropriateness, safety, guideline concordance, and potential role of AI-generated responses in healthcare consultation.
items.why: In a paired survey of 224 participants in Germany, an AI-generated (ChatGPT-4) response to a real health query was rated as more empathetic, comprehensible, and clinically accurate than a matched response written by a human physiotherapist, with all differences significant at p<.001. This is a genuine head-to-head comparison against a real clinician's answer, though it relies on a single query and exploratory cross-sectional design rather than a broader sample of clinical scenarios.
items.plain: Over 200 people compared an AI chatbot's answer to a health question against a real physiotherapist's answer to the same question, and rated the AI's response as clearer and more caring. This is a real test against an actual human clinician, but it's based on just one health question, so it's a small first look rather than a definitive comparison.

glossary.definition: A study that looks at a group of people at a single point in time rather than following them over time.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Assisted Self-Diagnosis and the Patient-Physician Relationship: Mixed Methods Study of Calibration, Participation, and Trust.
items.body: BACKGROUND: Patients increasingly use generative AI to interpret symptoms and seek health information, yet limited evidence shows how AI-assisted self-diagnosis is integrated into care-seeking and related to clinical interactions and patient-physician relationships. OBJECTIVE: This study examined how AI-assisted self-diagnosis is incorporated into care-seeking processes and how it relates to patient participation in clinical encounters and trust in physicians. METHODS: An exploratory sequential mixed methods design was used. In the qualitative phase, Chinese adults who had used generative AI to interpret symptoms, appraise possible conditions, or seek health advice within the previous year were purposively recruited through Xiaohongshu, WeChat Moments, and WeChat groups. Semistructured interviews were conducted from August 20, 2025, to January 10, 2026, and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. In the quantitative phase, an anonymous web-based survey was conducted in China through Huixiang Data from January 25, 2026, through January 28, 2026. Adults who had used generative AI for health consultation involving symptom interpretation or preliminary self-diagnosis within the previous 6 months were recruited through convenience sampling. Measures included perceived AI-assisted self-diagnosis quality, calibrated illness appraisal, patient participation, diagnosis validation, diagnosis comprehension, trust in physicians, AI use frequency, trust in health information sources, and demographic characteristics. Trust in physicians was assessed using 5 adapted items covering competence, integrity, and benevolence. Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, and PROCESS mediation analyses were performed. RESULTS: Qualitative findings (n=48) indicated that AI-assisted self-diagnosis was commonly used in a prediagnostic gray zone for preliminary orientation, informal triage, and interim self-management. Participants described AI as helping them appraise illness severity, prepare for consultations, ask questions, and understand physicians' diagnoses and reasoning. Quantitative findings (n=546) were consistent with these patterns. Perceived AI quality was positively associated with calibrated illness appraisal (=0.57, 95% CI 0.49-0.64), which was positively associated with patient participation (=0.35, 95% CI 0.28-0.43). The indirect association was significant (estimate=0.20, 95% bootstrap CI 0.14-0.26). Perceived AI quality was also associated with diagnosis validation (=0.69, 95% CI 0.61-0.76) and diagnosis comprehension (=0.65, 95% CI 0.58-0.73), which were associated with trust in physicians (=0.15, 95% CI 0.07-0.23 and=0.20, 95% CI 0.12-0.28, respectively). The corresponding indirect associations were 0.10 (95% bootstrap CI 0.04-0.17) through diagnosis validation and 0.13 (95% bootstrap CI 0.07-0.19) through diagnosis comprehension. CONCLUSIONS: Generative AI may function as an informational intermediary across the care-seeking process rather than undermine medical authority. By supporting illness appraisal, consultation preparation, and postconsultation understanding, AI-assisted self-diagnosis may be associated with greater patient participation and trust in physicians.
items.why: A mixed-methods study combining qualitative interviews (n=48) and a quantitative survey (n=546) examined how generative artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted self-diagnosis relates to patient participation and trust in physicians, finding that perceived AI quality was positively associated with calibrated illness appraisal, which in turn predicted patient participation in clinical encounters (indirect effect estimate=0.20). This offers a measured look at real behavioral and relational effects of AI use on the patient-physician relationship, though it relies on self-report and correlational survey data rather than an intervention.
items.plain: Researchers surveyed and interviewed hundreds of people in China who had used AI chatbots to try to figure out what was wrong with them, and found that when people trusted the AI's assessment more, they participated more actively in later doctor visits. This is a real look at how AI use is changing patient behavior with doctors, though it only shows correlations, not proof that the AI caused the change.

glossary.definition: AI systems that can produce new text, images, or other content rather than just classify existing data.
A research approach that combines numerical survey data with in-depth interviews to get a fuller picture.

items.title: Vocal Cord Dysfunction: Evaluating the Utility of AI Large Language Models for Patient Education.
items.source: World J Otorhinolaryngol Head Neck Surg
items.body: OBJECTIVE: To compare provider preferences for patient education materials generated by OpenEvidence, ChatGPT 5 Extended Thinking, and a laryngologist with fellowship training in response to common patient questions about vocal cord dysfunction (VCD). STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional survey study. METHODS: A laryngologist compiled four common patient questions about VCD and authored expert responses. Equivalent responses for patients were generated using OpenEvidence and ChatGPT 5 Extended Thinking with a standardized role prompt, each in a new chat session, and all outputs were limited to four sentences. Responses were de-identified and presented in a REDCap survey. Forty-five healthcare providers ranked responses based on perceived medical accuracy, clarity, and ability to address patient concerns. Preferences were analyzed using chi-square goodness-of-fit and Friedman testing with post hoc pairwise comparisons. RESULTS: Among the 45 respondents, the most represented specialties were otolaryngology ( = 17) and allergy/immunology ( = 12), and most were attending physicians ( = 31). ChatGPT 5 Extended Thinking received the most first choice selections for three of the four questions, whereas OpenEvidence and ChatGPT performed similarly on the definition question. Analyses of full rankings confirmed significant differences among sources for all four questions (all Friedman ≤ 0.001): responses generated by AI were preferred over the laryngologist response for the definition, diagnosis, and treatment process questions, while ChatGPT was preferred over both comparators for the etiology question. Otolaryngology respondents were more likely than non-otolaryngology respondents to rank the laryngologist response first for the definition question only. CONCLUSION: Responses generated by AI were frequently preferred over a single expert comparator for common VCD questions, with ChatGPT 5 Extended Thinking performing best overall and OpenEvidence showing similar performance on several items. These findings support further evaluation of LLMs as adjunctive tools in laryngology patient education, while highlighting the need for clinician oversight, assessment of individual model performance, and studies of patient outcomes.
items.why: A cross-sectional survey had 45 healthcare providers rank patient-education responses about vocal cord dysfunction (VCD) from a laryngologist versus two chatbots, finding AI-generated answers were preferred over the human expert for three of four questions (Friedman p<=.001). This is a genuine head-to-head comparison against a real clinician, though it uses provider rather than patient raters and only four questions, limiting generalizability.
items.plain: Doctors and other health providers compared answers about a voice disorder written either by a specialist doctor or by AI chatbots, and often preferred the AI's answers. It is a real test against a human expert, but it only involved four questions and provider judges rather than patients.

glossary.definition: A statistical test used to compare rankings across three or more related groups, such as multiple raters ranking several options.

items.title: Menopausal Hormone Therapy Linked to 35% Lower Alzheimer’s Risk
items.body: A recent study by Stanford Medicine, funded by the National Institutes of Health, found that women using estrogen-only menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) had 35% lower odds of Alzheimer’s disease and 39% lower odds of any dementia diagnosis. The study examined two databases of 21,462 participants, including an autopsy arm of 258 women who had used estrogen-only MHT compared with 2,701 non-users. Alongside… The post Menopausal Hormone Therapy Linked to 35% Lower Alzheimer’s Risk first appeared on .
items.why: A Stanford Medicine study funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) examined two databases totaling 21,462 participants and found estrogen-only menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) associated with 35% lower odds of Alzheimer's disease and 39% lower odds of any dementia diagnosis, including an autopsy-confirmed subgroup of 258 users versus 2,701 non-users. This is a substantive observational finding with real effect sizes and a notable autopsy-validated subgroup, though as an industry-beat item it should be read as an association from observational data rather than a randomized trial establishing causation.
items.plain: A study of over 21,000 women found that those who used a specific type of hormone therapy after menopause had a 35% lower chance of developing Alzheimer's disease and a 39% lower chance of any dementia. This is a real finding with solid numbers, but since it comes from observing existing patient records rather than a controlled experiment, it shows a strong association, not proof that the hormone therapy directly causes lower dementia risk.

Treatment using hormones like estrogen to relieve symptoms of menopause.
A way of expressing how likely an event is to happen compared to it not happening, often reported as a ratio between two groups.

items.title: The Invisible Workforce: An Algorithmic Audit of Nursing, Primary Care, and Holistic Gaps in AI-Generated Survivorship Plans.
items.body: OBJECTIVES: Advanced ovarian cancer survivorship requires multidisciplinary coordination. As patients use large language models (LLMs) as clinical navigators, essential professional roles may be inconsistently represented. This study evaluates the comprehensiveness, professional attribution, and readability of LLM-generated survivorship plans. METHODS: An algorithmic audit (N = 50) queried ChatGPT-5.1 using a standardized persona: a 58-year-old advanced ovarian cancer survivor. A dual-layer content analysis assessed nine guideline-derived domains, distinguishing explicit professional attribution from implicit functional guidance. A Nursing Function Layer quantified implicit nursing content. Readability was measured via the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level. RESULTS: Medical Oncology achieved 100% explicit attribution. Conversely, Primary Care was explicitly referenced in 2% (implicit: 14%), Genetic Counseling in 0%, and Nursing in 14% (implicit: 80%), revealing a 66-point attribution gap. Despite low explicit professional attribution, nursing-relevant functional content appeared in 96% of responses (mean = 4.16 functions/response). Responses averaged an 11.57 Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, substantially exceeding the sixth- to eighth-grade literacy benchmark. CONCLUSIONS: LLMs demonstrate high biomedical content coverage but systematically underrepresent holistic care professionals. The functional presence of nursing content without professional visibility highlights algorithmic bias. Unsupervised LLM use risks fragmented survivorship guidance, necessitating "nurse-in-the-loop" validation workflows to correct attribution gaps and calibrate literacy levels. IMPLICATIONS FOR NURSING PRACTICE: AI-generated survivorship plans reflect a purely biomedical focus, systematically omitting primary care integration (2%) and explicit nursing roles (14%). This structural fragmentation necessitates "nurse-in-the-loop" workflows, positioning oncology nurses to actively review AI outputs, activate neglected primary care referrals for comorbidity management, and calibrate reading difficulty to safe patient literacy levels.
items.why: An algorithmic audit of 50 ChatGPT-5.1-generated ovarian cancer survivorship plans found systematic underrepresentation of primary care and nursing roles (explicit attribution of 2% and 14% respectively) despite substantial implicit functional content, alongside reading levels above recommended patient literacy benchmarks. This surfaces a concrete failure mode, systematic omission of holistic care roles, relevant to understanding risks of unsupervised patient-facing LLM use, though it examines only one model and no clinician comparator.
items.plain: Researchers asked an AI chatbot fifty times to generate a care plan for an ovarian cancer survivor and found it almost never mentioned nurses or primary care doctors by name, even though it often included the kind of advice those professionals would give. This reveals a specific blind spot in how AI describes a care team, though only one AI model was tested.

glossary.definition: A systematic check of an AI system's outputs to look for patterns of bias or missing content.

items.title: NIH Launches $1.3M Maternal Health Research Challenge
items.body: The NIH has teamed up with crowdsourcing platform HeroX to launch a $1.3 million maternal health research challenge: Connecting the Community for Maternal Health Challenge 2.0: Research Capacity Building in Maternity Care Deserts. items.why: The National Institutes of Health (NIH) launched a $1.3 million crowdsourced research challenge through HeroX targeting maternal health research capacity in maternity care deserts, aimed at community, tribal, and faith-based organizations. This is a concrete, specifically funded federal initiative addressing a real access gap, though it is a challenge structure rather than a completed study or product.
items.plain: The US National Institutes of Health is offering $1.3 million in prize funding for community groups to research ways to improve maternal health care in areas that lack it. This is real money committed to a specific problem, though it's just the start of a competition, not a finished solution.

items.title: OBstat Expands Nationwide to Address OB/GYN Staffing Gaps
items.body: Flexible staffing platform OBstat has expanded nationwide to increase access to short-term and transitional clinician coverage across maternal healthcare. OBstat, a locum tenens staffing company designed specifically for OB/GYN clinicians, launched in 2024 to support women’s health services company Ob Hospitalist Group – which provides maternal health solutions and operates a maternal-fetal telehealth platform. OBstat recruits, vets, and schedules clinicians to fill… The post OBstat Expands Nationwide to Address OB/GYN Staffing Gaps first appeared on .
items.why: OBstat, a locum tenens staffing platform for obstetrics and gynecology (OB/GYN) clinicians affiliated with Ob Hospitalist Group, announced nationwide expansion to fill short-term staffing gaps in maternal healthcare. This is a concrete operational expansion addressing a real workforce shortage, though it involves no new clinical or regulatory milestone.
items.plain: A company that provides temporary doctors to fill staffing gaps in women's health clinics has expanded across the whole country. This is a real business expansion addressing a genuine shortage of OB/GYN doctors, though it isn't a new medical breakthrough.

items.title: Biograph Debuts Women’s Health Program to Advance Lifestage Care
items.body: Preventive health clinic Biograph has launched its Women’s Health Program to offer comprehensive care spanning women’s reproductive and hormonal lifestages. With clinics in New York City and the Bay Area, Biograph uses advanced diagnostics to create personalized, physician-led health care plans with ongoing monitoring. By bringing multiple specialties under one roof, the clinic aims to consolidate months of medical visits and referrals… The post Biograph Debuts Women’s Health Program to Advance Lifestage Care first appeared on .
items.why: Preventive health clinic Biograph launched a Women's Health Program combining advanced diagnostics with physician-led personalized care plans across its New York City and Bay Area locations. This is a real product and service launch consolidating care, though details on the diagnostics or clinical evidence behind them are not specified.
items.plain: A preventive health clinic chain has launched a new program specifically for women's reproductive and hormonal health, combining testing and doctor-led care plans in two US cities. This is a real new service being offered, though no data on its effectiveness is given.

scored.title: Large-scale AI-guided liver malignancy diagnosis: multicenter study and a single-arm trial.
scored.why: This large multicenter study developed LiON, a contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CE-CT) based AI system for liver malignancy diagnosis, validating it retrospectively across 22,251 patients (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) 0.975) and then testing it prospectively as an added reader in a single-arm trial of 10,333 patients, where it identified 51 previously overlooked lesions and prompted 22 multidisciplinary escalations. This is a rare example of AI moving from retrospective validation to real clinical workflow deployment with measurable downstream management changes, though it still needs a comparative prospective trial to establish outcome benefit.

scored.title: A bimodal large language model reduces misalignment in patient education: A double-blinded randomized trial.
scored.why: A double-blinded randomized controlled trial (RCT) tested a bimodal (text and audio) large language model (LLM), Dolphin, against a matched text-only LLM in patient education across 555 patients, finding higher patient satisfaction (98.6% vs 93.8%), greater suggestion acceptance (76.1% vs 58.9%), and fewer 7-day unplanned recontacts (12.9% vs 22.9%, p=0.002). This is a rare randomized trial with real clinical workload and satisfaction endpoints comparing an AI system against both a text-only AI and human educators, making it directly relevant evidence for whether multimodal cues improve patient communication.

scored.title: Prospective evaluation of a large language model clinical decision support system in the emergency department.
scored.why: In this DECIDE-AI stage 1 prospective evaluation, an emergency department deployed SHAKED, a large language model (LLM) based clinical decision support system, across 1,138 patients over four weeks, finding declining physician adoption (68% to 30%) tied to workload rather than any measured harm, with no significant change in length of stay. The key finding, that sustained clinician engagement rather than algorithmic accuracy is the bottleneck for AI adoption in acute care, is directly relevant to this reader's interest in how LLMs perform in real clinical use rather than in benchmark settings.

scored.title: Patient-Facing AI System for Symptom Guidance Using Simulated Encounters and Physician Review: Analytical Validation Study.
scored.why: A prospective predeployment validation study tested a locked configuration of a large language model (LLM)-enabled patient-facing symptom triage tool against 772 simulated cases with physician panel-derived ground truth, finding overtriage met the prespecified safety threshold (<30%) but urgent undertriage (6.9%) and nonurgent undertriage (18.4%) failed their respective thresholds. This is a real predeployment safety evaluation with quantified failure rates against explicit clinical criteria, directly relevant to assessing whether patient-facing symptom-guidance AI is safe enough for real use.

scored.title: User evaluation of AI- and human-generated responses in digital health communication: a paired survey study.
scored.why: In a paired survey of 224 participants in Germany, an AI-generated (ChatGPT-4) response to a real health query was rated as more empathetic, comprehensible, and clinically accurate than a matched response written by a human physiotherapist, with all differences significant at p<.001. This is a genuine head-to-head comparison against a real clinician's answer, though it relies on a single query and exploratory cross-sectional design rather than a broader sample of clinical scenarios.

scored.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Assisted Self-Diagnosis and the Patient-Physician Relationship: Mixed Methods Study of Calibration, Participation, and Trust.
scored.why: A mixed-methods study combining qualitative interviews (n=48) and a quantitative survey (n=546) examined how generative artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted self-diagnosis relates to patient participation and trust in physicians, finding that perceived AI quality was positively associated with calibrated illness appraisal, which in turn predicted patient participation in clinical encounters (indirect effect estimate=0.20). This offers a measured look at real behavioral and relational effects of AI use on the patient-physician relationship, though it relies on self-report and correlational survey data rather than an intervention.

scored.source: World J Otorhinolaryngol Head Neck Surg
scored.title: Vocal Cord Dysfunction: Evaluating the Utility of AI Large Language Models for Patient Education.
scored.why: A cross-sectional survey had 45 healthcare providers rank patient-education responses about vocal cord dysfunction (VCD) from a laryngologist versus two chatbots, finding AI-generated answers were preferred over the human expert for three of four questions (Friedman p<=.001). This is a genuine head-to-head comparison against a real clinician, though it uses provider rather than patient raters and only four questions, limiting generalizability.

scored.title: Menopausal Hormone Therapy Linked to 35% Lower Alzheimer’s Risk
scored.why: A Stanford Medicine study funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) examined two databases totaling 21,462 participants and found estrogen-only menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) associated with 35% lower odds of Alzheimer's disease and 39% lower odds of any dementia diagnosis, including an autopsy-confirmed subgroup of 258 users versus 2,701 non-users. This is a substantive observational finding with real effect sizes and a notable autopsy-validated subgroup, though as an industry-beat item it should be read as an association from observational data rather than a randomized trial establishing causation.

scored.title: The Invisible Workforce: An Algorithmic Audit of Nursing, Primary Care, and Holistic Gaps in AI-Generated Survivorship Plans.
scored.why: An algorithmic audit of 50 ChatGPT-5.1-generated ovarian cancer survivorship plans found systematic underrepresentation of primary care and nursing roles (explicit attribution of 2% and 14% respectively) despite substantial implicit functional content, alongside reading levels above recommended patient literacy benchmarks. This surfaces a concrete failure mode, systematic omission of holistic care roles, relevant to understanding risks of unsupervised patient-facing LLM use, though it examines only one model and no clinician comparator.

scored.title: NIH Launches $1.3M Maternal Health Research Challenge
scored.why: The National Institutes of Health (NIH) launched a $1.3 million crowdsourced research challenge through HeroX targeting maternal health research capacity in maternity care deserts, aimed at community, tribal, and faith-based organizations. This is a concrete, specifically funded federal initiative addressing a real access gap, though it is a challenge structure rather than a completed study or product.

scored.title: OBstat Expands Nationwide to Address OB/GYN Staffing Gaps
scored.why: OBstat, a locum tenens staffing platform for obstetrics and gynecology (OB/GYN) clinicians affiliated with Ob Hospitalist Group, announced nationwide expansion to fill short-term staffing gaps in maternal healthcare. This is a concrete operational expansion addressing a real workforce shortage, though it involves no new clinical or regulatory milestone.

scored.title: Biograph Debuts Women’s Health Program to Advance Lifestage Care
scored.why: Preventive health clinic Biograph launched a Women's Health Program combining advanced diagnostics with physician-led personalized care plans across its New York City and Bay Area locations. This is a real product and service launch consolidating care, though details on the diagnostics or clinical evidence behind them are not specified.

scored.title: Bird&Be Partners With Mandell’s Clinical Pharmacy to Expand Fertility Care Access
scored.why: Fertility supplement brand Bird&Be announced a partnership with Mandell's Clinical Pharmacy, a specialty fertility pharmacy, to expand distribution and referral access nationwide. This is a modest distribution partnership without new clinical, regulatory, or funding developments, so its market significance is limited.

scored.title: A scoping review on the mental health harms of LLM-based chatbots.
scored.why: This scoping review synthesizes 119 articles on potential mental health harms of large language model (LLM) based chatbots, categorizing findings into conceptual risks, vignette studies, and observational associations with overreliance or dependency. It is a synthesis without new primary data or clinician comparison, so it flags a landscape rather than delivering an actionable finding for this reader's beat on LLM-patient interaction.

scored.title: SMART: structured, meaningful, auditable, responsible, and transparent documentation for clinical AI.
scored.why: This paper introduces SMART, a documentation framework for clinical AI models that combines structured clinical vocabularies, lifecycle governance, and a blockchain-backed audit trail, evaluated through an illustrative case study and blockchain gas-usage experiments rather than real clinical deployment. It is an infrastructure proposal for AI governance rather than a study of AI performance or patient outcomes, so its relevance to this reader is limited to model-reporting practices.

scored.title: Accuracy and Safety of Language Model-Generated Breastfeeding Counseling Responses: An Expert-Based Comparative Evaluation of ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, and BreastfeedGPT.
scored.why: A comparative evaluation had eight breastfeeding experts rate responses from ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, and a customized domain-specific GPT (BreastfeedGPT) on ten frequently asked questions using Likert scales and the mDISCERN reliability instrument, finding the custom model scored highest on accuracy and tone. No human lactation consultant responses were included as a comparator, so this is a rubric-only comparison among chatbots rather than a test against real clinical practice.

scored.title: Ability of Large Language Models to Answer Patients' Questions and Generate Educational Materials for Uncommon Retinal Conditions.
scored.why: Retina specialists rated accuracy and completeness of three large language models (LLMs) answering 50 frequently asked questions on rare retinal diseases, and found models could lower reading grade level by 4-7 grades after being prompted to revise, without losing accuracy scores. There is no comparison against actual retina specialist answers or patient outcomes, so this remains a rubric-scored capability demonstration rather than evidence of clinical benefit.

scored.title: Comparative performance of artificial intelligence chatbots in patient education for robot-assisted radical prostatectomy: quality, transparency and readability.
scored.why: Four chatbots' patient-education responses about robot-assisted radical prostatectomy were scored on standardized quality instruments (DISCERN, EQIP, GQS, JAMA benchmark) and readability indices, with DeepSeek-V4 scoring highest but all models exceeding recommended reading levels. This is a model-versus-model comparison without any clinician-generated response as a baseline, so it is a routine benchmarking exercise rather than a test of real-world utility.

scored.title: Evaluation of AI Chatbot Responses to Pediatric Urology Frequently Asked Questions.
scored.why: Two board-certified pediatric urologists rated four large language models (LLMs) across seven quality domains for parent-facing frequently asked questions, finding generally high accuracy and safety scores but reading levels exceeding recommended patient-education standards. This is a rubric-based multi-model comparison without a human clinician response as a baseline, making it a routine benchmarking study.

scored.title: Are large language models such as ChatGPT, capable of supporting patients and general practitioners after spine surgery?
scored.why: Five large language models (LLMs) answered ten frequently asked spine surgery questions tailored to patients versus practitioners, with surgeons and lay raters scoring correctness, completeness, and empathy on Likert scales, finding ChatGPT and Claude scored highest for practitioner questions and Gemini and Copilot for patient-facing empathy and readability. This is a multi-model rubric comparison without a human clinician response as a comparator, so it demonstrates relative model performance rather than clinical utility.

scored.title: Menstrual Care Startup Sequel Taps WNBA Star Aliyah Boston As Co-Owner
scored.why: Menstrual care startup Sequel, maker of an FDA-approved spiral-design tampon, announced WNBA player Aliyah Boston as a co-owner, alongside noting prior funding of over $8 million. The core news here is a celebrity ownership addition rather than a new product, funding round, or regulatory action, placing it in the lower-value category of endorsement news.

scored.title: Midi Health Expands Beyond Menopause Care With New Brand Identity
scored.why: Women's telehealth platform Midi Health announced a new brand identity as it expands its clinical offerings beyond menopause care, referencing a previously reported $100 million funding round. The core news item is a rebrand, which per industry standards carries low signal value even though the company's underlying growth (450,000 patients served) is substantial.

scored.title: Building safer clinical agents: the case for residency-level benchmarks in medical artificial intelligence.
scored.why: This Lancet Digital Health piece argues for residency-level benchmarks to evaluate clinical AI agents, but no abstract or data is provided, so it appears to be an opinion or perspective article rather than an empirical study. Without evidence of a proposed benchmark's implementation or validation, it offers no measurable finding for this reader to act on.

scored.title: Ambient scribes as narrative technologies.
scored.why: This Lancet commentary argues, using medical humanities perspectives, that ambient scribes, AI-powered voice-to-text tools that document clinical encounters, should be understood as narrative technologies with under-recognized risks to patient-centered care. It presents no original data or evaluation, offering conceptual and policy recommendations rather than evidence this reader could weigh against other findings.

scored.title: Comparative Analysis of Large Language Model Outputs for Pre-hypnotherapy Support in Irritable Bowel Syndrome - An Experimental Feasibility Study.
scored.why: An exploratory feasibility study compared four large language models (LLMs) on readability and DISCERN information-quality scores for irritable bowel syndrome hypnotherapy questions, but used a single rater and explicitly states results cannot be considered definitive. This is a preliminary, likely underpowered comparison with no clinician benchmark and the authors themselves caution against drawing conclusions.

scored.title: On the risks of depersonalizing consent and the safe implementation of LLMs in medical decision-making.
scored.why: This is an ethics commentary responding to a prior proof-of-concept on large language model (LLM)-patient communication, arguing that removing human healthcare professionals from decision-making risks diminished autonomy, trust, and empathy. It contains no new empirical data or study design, functioning as opinion and commentary rather than evidence relevant to clinical practice.
